title: Before and after a decision
question: Around a contract approval or amendment, does the payee’s side deal more with the deciding official in the six months before than in the six months after, and more than with officials who neither decided nor voted on it?
finding: Across 3,760 approvals and amendments (2,443 with a named deciding or sponsoring official), the payee’s side dealt with the deciding official as follows. Donations: 37 in the 180 days before and 50 in the 180 days after (42% before). Gifts and trips: 2 in the 180 days before and 5 in the 180 days after (29% before). Lobbying contacts: 7 in the 180 days before and 5 in the 180 days after (58% before). With other supervisors sitting when the Board decided: donations: 149 in the 180 days before and 163 in the 180 days after (48% before). With officials and staff who neither decided, sponsored nor voted on it: donations: 742 in the 180 days before and 799 in the 180 days after (48% before); lobbying contacts: 993 in the 180 days before and 908 in the 180 days after (52% before). An even split is what unrelated timing would give.
how: For each approval or amendment (Board files that passed, and the City’s contract-approval notices), every donation, gift, lobbying contact and requested payment from the payee’s side within 180 days either side was counted, and sorted by the official on the other end: a sponsor of the Board file or the officer named as approving; another supervisor seen voting or sponsoring within 60 days of that date; or anyone else. Decisions inside 180 days of either end of the data are left out so both halves are complete, and so are Board decisions before 2014-01, the first month for which the records show who sat. A dealing near two decisions is counted with each; the last two columns count each dealing once.
limits: Donations follow the election calendar and contracts follow the budget calendar, so an uneven split can arise with no link between them; the comparison with officials who did not decide, and screen 3, are the checks. The City bars a contractor’s officers and directors from giving to an official who must approve its contract “from the submission of a proposal for a contract until twelve months from the date the contract was approved” (Ethics Commission guidance quoted in this project’s case file on contract-window donations), which by itself would thin out donations just after an approval. Every supervisor votes on a Board file, so “other supervisors” still had a vote, and the third group includes department heads and staff, who negotiate contracts without deciding them. A sponsor is printed on 55% of the Board’s money files (regularly from 2014); where none is printed, only the Mayor and other single officers are named. Lobbying before a decision is what lobbying is for, and is disclosed. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
